enrichment.short_title: GMC interim suspension appeal where inadequate IOC reasons but suspension upheld

statutes_considered.title: General Medical Council (Fitness to Practise and Other Procedures) Rules Order of Council 2000

key_facts: Dr Walker, already subject to a GMC condition prohibiting surgery after PCC proceedings concerning patient deaths, faced fresh criminal charges of manslaughter, theft of theatre records and perverting the course of justice.
The GMC Interim Orders Committee imposed an 18-month interim suspension in July 2003 on public-interest grounds pending disciplinary and criminal proceedings.

Walker appealed under section 41A(10), arguing the IOC's reasons were inadequate and the suspension disproportionate; new material emerged at the hearing about his Army employment and an unsigned police statement about the documents.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Statutory appeal under section 41A(10) of the Medical Act 1983 (treated as a full rehearing, not judicial review) against an IOC interim suspension order.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; court recommended IOC review the order in light of new material; Walker ordered to pay 60% of the GMC's costs.
enrichment.ratio: An appeal under section 41A(10) is a full rehearing on the merits, not Wednesbury review, but the court will normally give considerable weight to a professionally qualified IOC; inadequate reasons may invite closer scrutiny yet will not necessarily justify interference where serious pending charges warrant interim suspension.
legal_issues: Whether section 41A(10) creates a full appeal or merits review
Adequacy of brief oral/written reasons under Rule 14
Proportionality of interim suspension pending serious criminal charges
Effect of section 47(3) on employment during interim suspension
Whether judicial review remains available alongside the statutory appeal

key_facts: Mr Lewis claimed Mr Altaf unlawfully trespassed and caused nuisance by cutting overhanging trees so branches fell on his property at 40 Teme Road, Worcester.

enrichment.short_title: Asylum support certification upheld where gang witness could relocate within Jamaica
key_facts: Jamaican claimant returned to the UK under false names after removals and claimed asylum citing gang threats after witnessing a murder in Kingston.
Secretary of State refused asylum and human rights claims and certified them as clearly unfounded under section 94; Jamaica was designated under section 115(8).
Claimant gave a materially different asylum account in December 2002 (cousin's shooting) from that relied on in May 2003 (witness to murder of Taisa).
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of refusal and section 94 certification; limited permission granted (excluding Article 8); claimant appeared in person.
enrichment.outcome: Application for judicial review dismissed on relocation and, alternatively, credibility grounds.
enrichment.ratio: Even where state protection for targeted informers in Kingston may be insufficient on the evidence cited, certification can be upheld where relocation to another part of Jamaica (here Ocho Rios) would provide reasonable protection; wholly inconsistent prior asylum accounts may defeat credibility if the decision is quashed.
legal_issues: Application of the clearly unfounded test under section 94 after ZL
Sufficiency of state protection for non-state agent persecution (Horvath)
Whether relocation within Jamaica provides effective protection
Credibility where a different asylum narrative was previously given
Whether designation under section 115(8) alters the certification test

enrichment.short_title: Suspension of coffee arbitration enforcement conditional on US$400,000 security

statutes_considered.title: New York Convention on the Recognition and Enforcement of Foreign Arbitral Awards

key_facts: Swiss claimant Socadec obtained two London coffee-trade arbitration awards against Ugandan exporter Pan Afric Impex: approximately US$64,800 (quality) and US$646,000 (price on 35–36 contracts).

Morison J granted without-notice section 66 enforcement; defendant appealed late on the smaller award and timely on the larger, alleging time-bar under ECC Article 22 and disputing arbitrators' findings on fabricated faxes.
Defendant argued non-disclosure on the ex parte application, including claimant controller Timothy Espir's pending Swiss fraud charges.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application to set aside or suspend Morison J's order enforcing arbitration awards as judgments of the High Court.

enrichment.ratio: On an application to suspend section 66 enforcement pending appeal, the court applies Apis/Soleh Boneh principles: briefly assess validity of the award and enforcement difficulty; where the appeal has less than an even chance but is not manifestly hopeless, suspension on substantial security is appropriate.

enrichment.short_title: Trial in absence and section 142 rehearing refusal upheld for absent youth
key_facts: 19-year-old Afghan claimant jointly charged with indecent assault on a 14-year-old girl; co-defendant pleaded guilty before trial.
Claimant absent on 5 February 2003 despite notice; magistrates proceeded in absence, convicted on joint enterprise, and on 14 February refused to reopen under section 142.
Claimant pleaded guilty to bail offence for non-attendance; convicted and placed on Sex Offenders Register with conditional discharge.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review to quash magistrates' decisions to try in absence (5 February) and refuse rehearing (14 February).
enrichment.outcome: Application dismissed; both magistrates' decisions held within discretion.
enrichment.ratio: Applying Hayward principles (adapted for summary youth proceedings), trial in a defendant's absence is exceptional but may be justified where absence is deliberate, prosecution witnesses are present, and section 142 rehearing is refused when a Crown Court appeal rehearing remains available; brief magistrates' reasons need not mirror the full Hayward checklist if no clear error appears.

notes: Complete Court of Appeal judgment on Lloyd's PAYE coding and provisional loss relief.

enrichment.short_title: Lloyd's underwriting loss could not be reflected in PAYE code before loss sustained
key_facts: Lloyd's Name Keeling claimed expected underwriting loss of £425,390 (declared May 2003) should reduce his 2002/03 PAYE coding on pension income.
General Commissioners allowed appeal on provisional relief under section 203(7); High Court upheld relying on regulation 7(2)(f).
Under Finance Act 1993 section 172, losses declared in May 2003 correspond to tax year 2003/04 and were not yet 'sustained' when the code was set in 2002.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Revenue appeal to Court of Appeal against High Court decision upholding taxpayer's PAYE code appeal.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; inspector's PAYE code determination restored.
enrichment.ratio: Regulation 7(2)(a) limits PAYE codes to reliefs for which title is established at determination; a Lloyd's loss expected to be declared in a future underwriting year is not yet sustained under section 380 and cannot be provisionally deducted via regulation 7(2)(f) or section 203(7) without nullifying paragraph (a).

Whether PAYE coding may reflect anticipated future loss relief
Interaction of regulation 7(2)(a) and (f) and section 203(7)

notes: Complete judgment on section 55(5) asylum support and Article 3 destitution threshold.

enrichment.short_title: Asylum support refused where Iranian claimant not shown street-destitute under Article 3
key_facts: Iranian claimant arrived June 2003, claimed asylum late and was refused NASS support under section 55(1) for failing to claim promptly.
She relied on section 55(5) Article 3, asserting destitution if support withdrawn; adult British-citizen son had limited accommodation and income.
Screening interview recorded short stays with son and an Iranian acquaintance; further evidence gaps remained despite judicial review.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Permission and substantive hearing on judicial review of section 55(5) human-rights exemption (section 55(1) permission previously refused).
enrichment.outcome: Permission granted on section 55(5) point; relief refused and application dismissed; leave to appeal refused.
enrichment.ratio: Under section 55(5) the burden is on the applicant to show support is necessary to avoid Article 3 inhuman or degrading treatment; a high threshold requiring street homelessness or equivalent destitution is not met where family contacts, charitable assistance and unexplained gaps in the account leave a realistic possibility of alternative support.

Article 3 threshold for asylum support destitution (O, S D and T, Pretty)
Whether Secretary of State must formally reconsider when new evidence emerges

key_facts: 35-year-old Jorge Rodriguez-Bannister with Asperger's lived at isolated Hillside cottage with 55 hours/week one-to-one care funded by Somerset Trust.

Claimant's mother and Dr Shah favoured residential care; Trust preferred Dr Williams' supported-living model and panel recommendations.
